report.source_text: An incisional skin biopsy was taken and the histology demonstrated ulceration and an acanthotic epithelium, overlying a deep dermal inflammatory infiltrate comprising of neutrophils, lymphocytes, histiocytes and plasma cells (figure 2). There was no evidence of granulomas, vasculitis, malignancy or viral inclusions. Gram, DPAS, Grocott, Giemsa, Ziehl-Neelson and Wade-Fite special stains were all negative. The histological features were non-specific. Tissue bacterial and fungal cultures produced no significant growth, and Lesihmania PCR was negative.

Clinical course and response to treatment

report.source_text: Intravenous ceftazidime three times a day with oral co-trimoxazole (160 mg/800 mg) one tablet two times a day was started. Fucibet cream (a combined topical potent corticosteroid and fusidic acid), along with various wound dressings were used with no significant effect. Once a diagnosis of CM was made, the dose of co-trimoxazole was increased to the recommended (160 mg/800 mg) two tablets two times a day with folic acid supplementation for 3 months. The topical corticosteroid was stopped. Our specialist dermatology nurse debrided and dressed the wound with a negative pressure dressing on a weekly basis for several weeks. The patient was then taught how to manage the negative pressure dressing.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Cutaneous Melioidosis (CM) caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 26-year-old man presented with chronic distal left leg ulceration after extensive travel in Southeast Asia. Initial wound swab identified Burkholderia thailandensis (E004). An incisional skin biopsy showed non-specific inflammation with negative cultures and special stains, ruling out several alternative diagnoses (E003). The initial identification of B. thailandensis was questioned due to an unusual antibiotic susceptibility profile, which made Burkholderia pseudomallei a more likely culprit (E005). Treatment was initiated with intravenous ceftazidime and oral co-trimoxazole, with the co-trimoxazole dose subsequently increased to recommended levels for melioidosis (E006). Within 3 weeks of the adjusted treatment, the ulcers re-epithelialized with scarring, and there has been no recurrence after 20 months (E007).

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with chronic distal left leg ulceration after extensive travel in Southeast Asia, consistent with exposure to endemic areas for melioidosis.

Initial microbiological identification of Burkholderia thailandensis was re-evaluated due to an unusual antibiotic susceptibility profile, suggesting Burkholderia pseudomallei as the causative organism.
Histopathology from skin biopsy showed non-specific inflammation, ruling out granulomas, vasculitis, malignancy, and other specific infections.
Treatment was initiated and adjusted to a regimen appropriate for melioidosis (ceftazidime and high-dose co-trimoxazole).
Significant clinical improvement with re-epithelialization of ulcers and no recurrence after 20 months was observed following melioidosis-specific treatment.
